analysis.investment_thesis: Cello World is a decent-quality business with ROCE of 23.7%, but at current prices the earnings yield (~5.4% EBIT/EV) falls below my 6% Magic Formula threshold, meaning you're paying full price for a good-but-not-great compounder. Wait for a meaningful price correction before initiating a position.
key_strengths: High ROCE of 23.7% sustained over multiple years — passes the 'good business' half of the Magic Formula
Near-zero debt (borrowings collapsed from INR 334 Cr to INR 6 Cr) with 75% promoter skin-in-the-game
Consistent revenue (19.5% CAGR) and net profit (21.8% CAGR) growth over 4 years
key_risks: Earnings yield of ~5.4% (EBIT INR 510 Cr / EV ~INR 9,485 Cr) is below the Magic Formula's 6% floor — stock is not cheap
Poor FCF conversion: OCF of INR 262 Cr vs net profit of INR 365 Cr (72%), with FCF only INR 98 Cr — heavy capex cycle (INR 167–264 Cr/yr) is consuming earnings
Highly fragmented, commoditized categories (plasticware, glassware, appliances) with no clear pricing power moat — margins could compress from competition
red_flags: Other income surged to INR 45 Cr (2025) from INR 10 Cr (2021) — inflating reported net profit; strip this out and core earnings quality is weaker

Investing outflows of INR 553 Cr in FY25 vs OCF of only INR 262 Cr — company is spending nearly 2x its operating cash, funded by equity raise (financing CF +INR 311 Cr), diluting the return-on-capital story
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Cello World: EBIT (FY25 Operating Income) = INR 510 Cr; Enterprise Value ≈ INR 9,532 Cr market cap + INR 5 Cr debt – INR 52 Cr cash = ~INR 9,485 Cr. Earnings Yield = 5.4% — below my 6% minimum. ROCE of 23.7% (provided) is solid and crosses the 20% hurdle for "good business," but one good metric alone doesn't make a Magic Formula buy. The EV/EBITDA of 17.2x confirms the market is not offering a bargain here — you need both halves of the formula to work simultaneously.

The FCF story is concerning for a supposed asset-light consumer brand. Free cash flow of only INR 98 Cr against net profit of INR 365 Cr (27% conversion) signals heavy capital reinvestment — capex averaged INR 167–264 Cr over the last two years. The CWIP spike to INR 180 Cr in FY24 (now drawn down to INR 51 Cr) suggests a new capacity cycle. If this capex doesn't generate incremental ROIC above cost of capital, the Magic Formula rank deteriorates further. At a P/E of 30x current and 24x forward, the stock needs flawless execution with no margin compression — a bar too high for me to underwrite at today's price.
